summary: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water from six large stone jars into the best wine of the feast, His first sign, and His disciples believe in Him.
key_insight: John tells us what the six jars were for: “the manner of purification of the Jews.” Jesus took vessels meant for ritual washing and filled them with the best wine of the feast. What He brings does not patch up the old; it surpasses it.
story: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. The mother of Jesus was there, and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited.

When the wine ran out, His mother said to Him, “They have no wine.” Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does your concern have to do with Me? My hour has not yet come.” His mother said to the servants, “Whatever He says to you, do it.”

Six stone waterpots stood nearby, used for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the waterpots with water.” They filled them up to the brim. Then He said, “Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast.” And they took it.

The master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine. He did not know where it had come from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew. He called the bridegroom and said, “Every man at the beginning sets out the good wine, and when the guests have well drunk, then the inferior. You have kept the good wine until now!”
This was the beginning of Jesus’ signs, done in Cana of Galilee. In it He revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.

scene.label: A village wedding
scene.text: A wedding was a feast for the whole community and could last several days, like Samson’s seven-day feast (Judges 14:12). The groom’s family provided the food and wine. Running out would bring real shame on the family in front of the whole village.

scene.label: “Woman”
scene.text: This was not rude. It was a respectful form of address, and Jesus used it again for His mother from the cross (John 19:26). Still, His words set a distance: what He did would be ruled by His “hour,” not by a family request.

scene.label: Stone waterpots
scene.text: Stone jars were used for purification water because stone, unlike pottery, was thought not to become ritually unclean. Archaeologists have found many such vessels from this period in Galilee and Judea. Six jars of twenty to thirty gallons held about 120 to 180 gallons.

scene.label: The master of the feast
scene.text: He was the guest or head servant in charge of the banquet, who tasted the wine and directed the serving. He was the one person in a position to judge the wine, and he did not know where it came from.

scene.label: Wine in the prophets
scene.text: The prophets pictured the coming day of God’s blessing as a feast with abundant wine: “The mountains shall drip with sweet wine” (Amos 9:13; see also Isaiah 25:6).

witnesses.john: Only John tells this sign, and he calls it the “beginning of signs.” It opens a series of signs John chose and wrote down “that you may believe” (John 20:31). Mary appears at this first sign and again at the cross, and both times Jesus addresses her as “Woman” (19:26).

seeing.reveals: Jesus first reveals His glory not in the temple or before crowds, but at a village wedding, quietly saving a family from shame with more than enough of the best.
seeing.living: Mary brought the need to Jesus and then left the how and the when to Him: “Whatever He says to you, do it.” The servants obeyed an order that seemed pointless, filling jars with water, and they were the ones who knew where the wine came from. Those who obey Him in plain things see what others only taste.
seeing.ponder: What need have you brought to Jesus, and are you willing to leave the how and the when with Him?

preaching.big_idea: Bring the need to Jesus, do whatever He says, and watch Him reveal His glory.
preaching.watch_for: “My hour has not yet come” (2:4) begins a thread that runs through John (7:30; 8:20) until Jesus says, “The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified” (12:23). The glory shown at Cana points ahead to the glory of the cross.
